title: Newton's Law of Cooling — Derivation of Rate of Fall of Temperature
notes: Newton's law of cooling says that, when the excess temperature is not large, the rate of loss of heat is proportional to the excess of the body's temperature over the surroundings.
If the heat loss is dQ in time dt, then dQ/dt = K (θ − θ0), where K depends on the exposed area and the nature of the surface, and θ0 is the surrounding temperature.
The heat leaving the body also equals −mc dθ, if the body cools without changing state. Dividing by dt gives −mc dθ/dt = K (θ − θ0).
Therefore the rate of fall of temperature is dθ/dt = −(K/mc) (θ − θ0). The constant k = K/(mc) is larger when the body has a small heat capacity.
The minus sign means the temperature falls when θ is above θ0. If the body is cooler than the room, the same equation makes the temperature rise.

The law is a linear approximation. It is used for excesses of a few tens of degrees, where convection and a linearised radiation loss dominate. A red-hot body needs the Stefan–Boltzmann difference of fourth powers.

exercises.question: Two bodies have the same surface constant K and the same excess temperature. Their heat capacities are mc and 2mc. Compare the initial rates of fall of temperature.
steps: For the first body the magnitude of the rate is (K/mc) times the excess.
For the second body the heat capacity is doubled, so the magnitude is half as large.
The excess and K are the same, so they cancel in the comparison.
The first body cools twice as fast in temperature.
exercises.answer: The body with heat capacity mc has twice the initial rate of fall of the body with 2mc.
